name: Feldenkrais Method

card.summary: Gentle somatic movement education aimed at body awareness and efficient movement; reviews find no conclusive evidence of medical benefit, and posture looks are untested.
card.note: Reviews report no conclusive evidence of medical benefit; researchers do not consider it to pose serious risks.

quick.overview:
The Feldenkrais Method is a movement-education system created by Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). It is taught in verbally guided group classes (Awareness Through Movement) and one-to-one hands-on sessions (Functional Integration).

Proponents say it improves awareness and ease of movement, and it is sometimes mentioned in posture discussions. Reviews describe no conclusive evidence of medical benefit, with some small trials in chronic low back pain; no study found tests it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say slow, exploratory movement and attention to sensation help the nervous system learn new movement patterns. Some researchers link the method to dynamic systems theory of motor behaviour.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says researchers do not believe the method poses serious risks. Critics, including physician David Gorski, have compared it to faith healing, and Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness.

lead: The Feldenkrais Method is a form of somatic education devised by Israeli physicist and judo expert Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). It teaches people to notice and vary habitual movement patterns, with the aim of easier, more efficient movement and better body awareness; people interested in posture and how they carry themselves use it for that reason. Its two formats are Awareness Through Movement, verbally guided group lessons, and Functional Integration, hands-on individual sessions.[1][2]

Proponents say it improves movement quality and awareness and can repair impaired connections between the brain and the body.[2] Research consists of small randomised trials and systematic reviews in groups such as people with chronic low back pain and older adults, with gait, balance and pain as typical outcomes.[3][4][5][14] A 2015 Australian government review of private-health-insurance subsidies, which covered 16 therapies, found no clear evidence of effectiveness and the method was excluded from subsidies in 2017, according to Wikipedia.[2] No study found tests it with posture appearance as an outcome.
infobox: Small randomised trials and systematic reviews

paras: Lessons are built on five principles listed in accounts of the method: learning as a process, posture as dynamic equilibrium, exploratory rather than performative movement, learning about the whole rather than the part, and repetition with variation.[2] In Awareness Through Movement, a teacher talks a group through slow movement sequences, often lying on the floor, and invites students to attend to sensation rather than to reach a target position. In Functional Integration, a practitioner uses touch and gentle guided movement with one person.[2]

Posture is one of the topics proponents raise, and the Wikipedia account describes the method as increasingly used by musicians, actors, dancers and athletes who want refined control of movement.[2] People discussing posture and presence online sometimes mention it as a way to learn less effortful alignment; this rests on practitioner and user reports rather than measured appearance outcomes.

Proponents also describe benefits for conditions such as multiple sclerosis and autism spectrum disorders, claims a 2014 review in Wisconsin reported had no supporting studies identifying participants with those conditions.[2]

Feldenkrais was born in Slavuta and studied engineering and physics in Paris, where he practised judo. After a knee injury in 1940s Britain, he experimented with gentle movement. He published Body and Mature Behaviour in 1949 and taught in Tel Aviv from the early 1950s.[1] He taught practitioners in San Francisco and Amherst trainings, and the International Feldenkrais Federation was founded in 1994.[1][2]

Feldenkrais taught in Tel Aviv from the 1950s until his death, and media coverage of his work with Israeli prime minister David Ben-Gurion is credited with building his reputation.[2] From the late 1950s he also taught in Europe and America. Several hundred people qualified as practitioners in training programs in San Francisco (1975 to 1978) and Amherst, Massachusetts (1980 to 1984).[2] A 2007 biography by David Kaetz, Making Connections, traces links between his Jewish upbringing and his teaching style, such as the use of paradox, and from the 1990s dynamic systems theory, through researcher Esther Thelen, shaped how the method has been explained.[2]

Moshe Feldenkrais was born on 6 May 1904 in Slavuta, then in the Russian Empire and now in Ukraine, was raised in Baranovichi, and emigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1918.[16] He later earned an engineering degree in France and a physics doctorate at the University of Paris, where Marie Curie was among his teachers, and worked as a research assistant to Frederic Joliot-Curie at the Radium Institute.[16]

His interest in movement came through martial arts. He studied ju-jitsu in Palestine, met the judo founder Jigoro Kano in Paris in 1933, and co-founded the Ju-Jitsu Club de France.[16] A soccer knee injury in 1929 that was aggravated during the Second World War led him to develop self-observation and self-rehabilitation methods, and these grew into the method that bears his name.[16] After fleeing France for Britain in 1940 he served as a science officer in the Admiralty until 1946 on anti-submarine and sonar work, and he published Body and Mature Behavior in 1949.[16]

He returned to Israel in 1951, settled in Tel Aviv in 1954 and taught full time. Press accounts of his sessions with Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion, whom he is reported to have taught to stand on his head, helped his reputation spread.[16][2] From the 1960s to the 1980s he taught in Europe and North America, including at Esalen in 1972 and Hampshire College in 1980, and he stopped public teaching after becoming ill in 1981; he died in Tel Aviv on 1 July 1984, aged 80.[16] His central premise, as summarised on Wikipedia, was that thought, feeling, perception and movement are closely interrelated and influence each other.[16]

Accounts of the method list five principles: learning is a process driven by sensory and kinesthetic information from interacting with the environment; posture is a dynamic equilibrium, meaning the ability to regain balance after a large disturbance; movement can be exploratory or performative, with attention to ease and quality; learning moves between whole actions and their parts; and repetition with variation widens the options a person can choose from.[2]

Awareness Through Movement lessons are verbally guided and practised in groups. Functional Integration lessons are hands-on, one-to-one sessions in which the practitioner guides the student's movement through touch.[2]

sections.h: How people use it for posture and appearance
paras: For people interested in how they carry themselves, the method's appeal is that it addresses posture as a skill of movement rather than a fixed position. Proponents describe the aim as less habitual muscular holding, a freer neck and shoulders, and a more balanced stance and gait, which together are read from the outside as a more upright, relaxed presence.[2]

The method is also used by people whose work depends on how they look in motion. The Oxford Handbook of Music Performance, as quoted on Wikipedia, describes growing use among musicians, actors, dancers and athletes who want refined control of movement.[2] Feldenkrais lessons are taught in classes and workshops by practitioners certified through programmes that began with trainings Feldenkrais himself held in San Francisco from 1975 to 1978 and in Amherst, Massachusetts from 1980 to 1984, which certified several hundred people.[2]

Wikipedia reports that a 2022 report from Germany's IQWiG found a hint of benefit in Parkinson disease compared with a passive lecture programme, inconsistent results for chronic low back pain and no long-term benefit, and described the overall evidence as limited with few ongoing randomised trials.[2] Claimed benefits for autism spectrum disorders and multiple sclerosis are described there as lacking supporting studies.[2]

A 2015 Australian government review of natural therapies for private-health-insurance subsidy covered 16 therapies, found no clear evidence of effectiveness for the Feldenkrais Method, and the method was excluded from the subsidy in 2017, according to the same account.[2] Practitioners and supporters respond that the method is aimed at learning and awareness rather than treating disease.[2]

A 2017 single-blind randomised trial of 53 patients with chronic low back pain compared the method with Back School for pain and interoceptive awareness, and a 2020 randomised trial compared it with core stability exercise.[6][7] A 1999 controlled study examined Feldenkrais bodywork versus sham in multiple sclerosis.[8]

A 2015 systematic review and a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials assessed its effectiveness as a physiotherapy tool.[4][5] A 2022 German IQWiG report, per Wikipedia, found a hint of benefit in Parkinson disease and inconsistent results for chronic low back pain without long-term benefit evidence.[2] No studies found testing posture appearance as an outcome.

The 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials reported that in older adults, three of four trials found improved gait, balance, mobility and quality of life, and the pooled Timed-Up-and-Go result favoured the method (Cohen's d about -1.14). In trials of neck, upper back or shoulder pain, pain, functional balance and perceived exertion improved, and in three chronic low back pain trials pain, disability, quality of life and interoceptive awareness improved.[5]

Additional trials include an eight-week randomised trial in 30 older women with chronic low back pain comparing stabilization exercise with and without Feldenkrais,[10] trials of balance and postural control in older adults with diabetic neuropathy,[11][13] a randomised trial in people with intellectual disability,[12] and a proof-of-concept study in fibromyalgia.[15] A 2022 German IQWiG report found, per Wikipedia, a hint of benefit in Parkinson disease compared with a passive lecture program and inconsistent results for chronic low back pain, with little evidence of long-term benefit.[2]

A 2009 study of the Feldenkrais method for balance in older adults examined effectiveness and acceptability, and a controlled, randomised trial of Feldenkrais-based exercise in people with Parkinson's disease reported improved quality of life.[17][18] These outcomes concern function, not looks.

David Gorski has compared the method to faith healing, and a consumer-health critic site lists it among unnaturalistic methods, as summarised on Wikipedia.[2] A review of bodywork trial methodology discusses bias control in this research area.[9]

Quackwatch lists it among unnaturalistic methods.[2] Practitioners and supporters respond that its aim is learning and awareness rather than treatment, and Wikipedia notes researchers do not consider it to pose serious risks.[2]

The International Feldenkrais Federation was founded in 1994, and national guilds such as the Feldenkrais Guild of North America describe the method as helping people regain an innate capacity for efficient movement.[1][2] Classes are offered as group lessons, workshops and private sessions, and the method is often compared with the Alexander technique in overviews of movement re-education.[3]

In strength and physique forums the method surfaces occasionally and briefly. A T Nation thread about movement systems jokes about a 'flame war' between Feldenkrais and Alexander technique followers, and another member suggests it as a gentle option for someone recovering from hemiparesis.[19][20] Both are casual remarks rather than programmes of use, and in looks-focused communities it appears mainly in posture and body-awareness conversations.

timeline.event: Moshe Feldenkrais is born in Slavuta. [16]
Feldenkrais meets judo founder Jigoro Kano in Paris. [16]
Feldenkrais publishes Body and Mature Behavior, the first book on his method. [16][1]
Settles in Tel Aviv and teaches full time. [16]
Feldenkrais begins a professional training in San Francisco (to 1978), followed by one in Amherst, Massachusetts (1980-1984). [2]
Feldenkrais dies in Tel Aviv on 1 July. [16]
Australian government review finds no clear evidence of effectiveness; the method is excluded from insurance subsidy in 2017. [2]

lore.intro: Feldenkrais is discussed by practitioners, performers and clients as a way of changing movement habits, and by critics as an alternative therapy; both views are recorded on its Wikipedia article.[2]

claims.claim: Slow awareness lessons improve posture and ease of movement
claims.believers: Practitioners say lessons build body awareness so that habitual tension is released and movement becomes more efficient, and performers use it for refined control.[2]
claims.experts: Randomised trials and systematic reviews examine pain, gait and balance in groups such as older adults and people with chronic low back pain, and a 2022 meta-analysis of 16 trials reported gait and balance gains in several older-adult trials; no study found tests posture appearance as an outcome.[5]

claims.claim: The method helps with conditions such as multiple sclerosis and autism
claims.believers: Proponents describe benefits for neurological conditions through improved brain-body connection.[2]
claims.experts: A review cited on Wikipedia reported no supporting studies identifying participants for these claims; a controlled bodywork study in multiple sclerosis exists.[2][8]

claims.claim: It is a legitimate learning method, not a treatment
claims.believers: Supporters state that its aim is learning and awareness rather than treating disease, and researchers do not consider it to pose serious risks.[2]
claims.experts: Critic David Gorski has likened it to faith healing, and Quackwatch lists it among unnaturalistic methods, as summarised on Wikipedia.[2]

claims.claim: Feldenkrais is a gentle option for people who cannot do conventional exercise.
claims.believers: A T Nation member suggested it as non-harmful and possibly helpful for someone with hemiparesis.[20]
claims.experts: Trials in older adults and Parkinson's disease report balance and quality-of-life gains, and Wikipedia notes researchers do not regard it as seriously risky.[17][18][2]

claims.claim: Feldenkrais and the Alexander technique are interchangeable.
claims.believers: Forum users group them together as movement-re-education methods.[19]
claims.experts: Clinical overviews compare the two in one review while describing them as distinct systems with different formats.[3]

angle.text: The method is used to change how a person holds and moves the body, which proponents link to freer, more upright carriage and smoother gait. Its appearance relevance runs through posture and movement quality rather than through any change to bones or tissue.
